newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada union won't extend Chrysler strike deadline.
newsitem.headline: Canada union won't extend Chrysler strike deadline.

text.p: The Canadian Auto Workers union said on Monday it will not extend its Tuesday midnight strike deadline against Chrysler Corp.'s Canadian unit, despite progress on the key issue of shifting work to outside suppliers.

CAW President Buzz Hargrove said time was running so short that even if the logjam over using outside suppliers, so-called outsourcing, could be broken, there might not be enough time before the deadline to resolve other contract issues.
Chrysler's lead negotiator, Ken Francese, "certainly has to indicate early today where he's going if he has any thought of doing this before the strike deadline," Hargrove told reporters.
The union has said its 12,600 Chrysler workers will strike the carmaker if an agreement is not reached by 11:59 p.m. EDT on Tuesday.
A collective agreement with Chrysler will become the framework for negotiations between the union and the Canadian units of General Motors Corp. and Ford Motor Co..
Hargrove said Chrysler negotiators were unwilling to meet overnight, saying they needed more time, but were likely to have discussions with the union later on Monday.

He said Chrysler's latest proposal on outsourcing, presented to the union on Sunday afternoon, recognised the principle of work ownership, but did not limit the automaker's ability to contract out the work.
"We own the work. The next step has to be that we have some say in what happens to it," said Hargrove.

"It (Chrysler) does now recognise the principle, in writing, of work ownership. But you could drive a truck through the language after that. So we are still an awful long ways apart," Hargrove said on Sunday during a break in bargaining.

CAW officials said work is owned by the union when workers are "producing quality products in a productive manner at reasonably low cost and (the company is) making a reasonable profit." Hargrove said once the company recognises work ownership, it follows that it cannot contract out the work without replacing it with other jobs.
Chrysler's Francese was unavailable on Monday but said on Sunday that he planned to meet again on the outsourcing issue and expected to begin closing the gap between the two sides.
"We're going to have more discussion on that and hopefully we'll be a lot closer at the end to resolving that issue," Francese said.
Hargrove said he had not expected Chrysler to concede the work ownership issue before a strike, but the early move to do so was only the first step toward controlling outsourcing.
"If you're looking down that tunnel, you'll see a little small light, but boy, it is faint," said Hargrove.
Hargrove said the union will not budge from its commitment to restrict outsourcing and that the talks cannot advance until the issue is settled.
Chrysler's stock rose 25 cents to $28.625 on the New York Stock Exchange in early afternoon trading.
